stem: The Indian landmass (subcontinent) is broadly divided into how many major physiographic divisions?
solution: The Indian landmass is broadly divided into six major physiographic (physical) divisions: (1) the Northern and North-eastern Mountains (the Himalayas); (2) the Northern Plains (the Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra plains); (3) the Peninsular Plateau; (4) the Indian Desert (the Thar); (5) the Coastal Plains; and (6) the Islands. Each division has its own distinctive relief, structure, and origin. Understanding that India has six major physiographic divisions is a prelims point. India has six major physiographic divisions: the Northern Mountains, the Northern Plains, the Peninsular Plateau, the Indian Desert, the Coastal Plains, and the Islands.

stem: The oldest and most stable landmass of India, made of ancient hard rocks and forming the Peninsular Plateau, is a part of the ancient supercontinent called:
solution: The Peninsular Plateau — the oldest and most stable part of the Indian landmass, made of ancient, hard igneous and metamorphic rocks — is a part of the ancient supercontinent of Gondwana (Gondwanaland), the southern part of the still-older supercontinent Pangaea. When Gondwana broke up, the Indian plate drifted north and collided with the Asian plate. So the Peninsular block is a very old, rigid, stable shield (one of the oldest landmasses on Earth), while the Himalayas and the Northern Plains are much younger features formed later. Understanding that the Peninsular Plateau is part of ancient Gondwana is a prelims point. The Peninsular Plateau is part of the ancient supercontinent Gondwana — India's oldest, most stable landmass.

stem: The Himalayas are __________ mountains (formed by the folding of sediments when two plates collided).
solution: The Himalayas are young fold mountains — geologically young mountains formed by the folding (buckling and uplift) of the thick sediments (that had accumulated in the Tethys Sea) when the northward-moving Indian plate collided with the Asian plate. Because they are young and still rising (the collision continues), the Himalayas are the highest and among the most rugged mountains in the world, and the region is tectonically active (prone to earthquakes). (This contrasts with the ancient, stable, worn-down Peninsular Plateau.) Understanding that the Himalayas are young fold mountains (from plate collision) is a key prelims point. The Himalayas are young fold mountains, formed by the collision of the Indian and Asian plates.

stem: The ancient sea, in whose sediments the Himalayas were later folded up, was called the:
solution: The Tethys Sea was the ancient sea that once lay between the Indian (Gondwana) landmass and the Asian (Angara/Laurasia) landmass. Over millions of years, thick layers of sediment accumulated on the floor of the Tethys Sea; when the northward-drifting Indian plate collided with the Asian plate, these sediments were compressed, folded, and uplifted to form the Himalayan mountains. So the Himalayas were literally raised out of the sediments of the former Tethys Sea (which is why marine fossils are found high in the Himalayas). Understanding the Tethys Sea (origin of the Himalayan sediments) is a prelims point. The Himalayas were folded up from the sediments of the ancient Tethys Sea.

stem: The Himalayas consist of three main parallel ranges. The northernmost, highest range (containing the loftiest peaks like Mount Everest) is the:
solution: The Himadri (also called the Great or Inner Himalayas, or the Himadri range) is the northernmost and highest of the three main parallel ranges of the Himalayas. It contains the loftiest peaks of the world, including Mount Everest, Kanchenjunga, and others (all above 6000 m on average), is perennially snow-covered, and has the great glaciers. It is the most continuous and rugged range, forming the backbone of the Himalayas. (The three ranges, from north to south, are: the Himadri (Great Himalayas), the Himachal (Lesser/Middle Himalayas), and the Shiwaliks (Outer Himalayas).) Understanding the Himadri (the highest, northernmost Himalayan range) is a prelims point. The Himadri (Great Himalayas) is the northernmost, highest range, containing the loftiest peaks like Mount Everest.

stem: The middle range of the Himalayas, lying between the Great Himalayas and the Shiwaliks (containing famous hill stations like Shimla, Mussoorie, and the valleys of Kashmir and Kangra), is the:
solution: The Himachal (also called the Lesser Himalayas, Middle Himalayas, or Himachal range) is the middle range of the Himalayas, lying between the lofty Himadri (Great Himalayas) to the north and the Shiwaliks (Outer Himalayas) to the south. Its ranges (like the Pir Panjal, Dhauladhar, and Mahabharat) are of medium height, and it contains many famous hill stations (Shimla, Mussoorie, Nainital, Darjeeling) and beautiful valleys (like the Kashmir Valley and the Kangra and Kullu valleys). Understanding the Himachal (Lesser Himalayas — hill stations and valleys) is a prelims point. The Himachal (Lesser Himalayas) is the middle Himalayan range, with famous hill stations and valleys.

stem: The southernmost, lowest range of the Himalayas (made of unconsolidated sediments brought down by the rivers) is the:
solution: The Shiwaliks (also called the Outer Himalayas or Sub-Himalayas) are the southernmost and lowest range of the three main Himalayan ranges. They are made largely of unconsolidated sediments (gravels, sands, and clays) brought down and deposited by the rivers flowing from the higher Himalayas. The Shiwaliks are the youngest part of the Himalayas. Between the Shiwaliks and the Lesser Himalayas lie flat-floored structural valleys called 'Duns' (like the Dehra Dun). Understanding the Shiwaliks (the lowest, outermost, sediment-made Himalayan range) is a prelims point. The Shiwaliks (Outer Himalayas) are the southernmost, lowest Himalayan range, made of river-deposited sediments.

stem: The flat-floored structural valleys (formed of gravel and alluvium) lying between the Lesser Himalayas and the Shiwaliks — like the Dehra Dun — are called:
solution: Duns (or 'Doons') are the flat-floored, longitudinal structural valleys that lie between the Lesser Himalayas (Himachal) and the Shiwaliks (Outer Himalayas). They are filled with gravel and alluvium (deposits). Famous examples include the Dehra Dun (the largest, in Uttarakhand), the Kotli Dun, and the Patli Dun. These valleys are fertile and often well-settled. Understanding Duns (the valleys between the Lesser Himalayas and the Shiwaliks) is a prelims point. Duns are the flat-floored valleys (like Dehra Dun) between the Lesser Himalayas and the Shiwaliks.

stem: The highest peak in India (and the third highest in the world), located in the eastern Himalayas (Sikkim), is:
solution: Kanchenjunga is the highest peak located within India (in Sikkim, on the India-Nepal border) and the third highest mountain in the world (about 8,586 m). (Mount Everest, the world's highest at 8,848 m, is in Nepal; and K2, the world's second highest, at about 8,611 m, is in the Karakoram range in the Pakistan-administered part of Kashmir — sometimes claimed as the highest peak in Indian territory as per India's claim on the region, but Kanchenjunga is the highest peak entirely within undisputed Indian territory.) Understanding that Kanchenjunga is the highest peak in India (3rd in the world) is a prelims point. Kanchenjunga (in Sikkim) is the highest peak in India and the third highest in the world.

stem: The hilly ranges of the north-eastern Himalayas (in the states of Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, etc.) are collectively called the:
solution: The Purvanchal (meaning 'Eastern Hills' or 'Eastern Mountains') are the hilly ranges of the north-eastern part of the Himalayas, where the Himalayas bend sharply southward and run along India's eastern border with Myanmar. They include ranges such as the Patkai Bum, the Naga Hills, the Manipur Hills, and the Mizo (Lushai) Hills — in the north-eastern states of Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, and Mizoram. These hills are lower than the main Himalayas and are covered with dense forests. Understanding the Purvanchal (the north-eastern hill ranges) is a prelims point. The Purvanchal are the eastern hill ranges of the north-eastern Himalayas (Naga, Manipur, Mizo hills, etc.).

stem: The Northern Plains of India are formed by the alluvial (sediment) deposits of three major river systems: the Indus, the Ganga, and the:
solution: The Northern Plains of India are formed by the alluvial deposits (silt, sand, and clay brought down and deposited by rivers) of three major river systems: the Indus, the Ganga, and the Brahmaputra (together with their many tributaries). Over millions of years, these rivers, flowing down from the Himalayas, filled a vast trough/depression with sediments, building up the flat, fertile Northern Plains. These plains are among the most fertile and densely populated regions of the world (the agricultural heartland of India). Understanding that the Northern Plains are built by the Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra is a prelims point. The Northern Plains are formed by the alluvium of the Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra river systems.

stem: The Northern Plains are famous for being extremely __________, which makes them the agricultural heartland of India.
options: fertile (rich in alluvial soil) and level
solution: The Northern Plains are famous for being extremely fertile (rich in deep alluvial soil, deposited by the rivers) and remarkably level/flat, which — together with plentiful water (from the perennial Himalayan rivers and groundwater) and a favourable climate — makes them highly productive for agriculture. This is why the Northern Plains are the agricultural heartland of India (the granary, producing much of the country's food grains) and one of the most intensively farmed and densely populated regions in the world. Understanding the fertility and importance of the Northern Plains is a prelims point. The Northern Plains are extremely fertile and level, making them the agricultural heartland of India.

stem: In the Northern Plains, the older alluvium (which forms terraces above the flood level, and is somewhat less fertile) is called:
solution: Bhangar is the older alluvium of the Northern Plains — it forms the higher terraces (above the flood level of the rivers), and it is generally darker, more clayey, and sometimes contains lime nodules (called 'kankar'). Being older and above the reach of the yearly floods, it is somewhat less fertile than the new alluvium. (The newer alluvium, deposited afresh by the floods each year, is called 'Khadar' — it is lighter, sandier, and more fertile.) Understanding Bhangar (the older, higher, less fertile alluvium) is a prelims point. Bhangar is the older alluvium of the Northern Plains, forming higher terraces above the flood level.

stem: In the Northern Plains, the newer, younger alluvium (deposited afresh by floods each year in the lowlands near the rivers, and very fertile) is called:
solution: Khadar is the newer, younger alluvium of the Northern Plains — it is found in the low-lying areas near the rivers, where it is deposited afresh (renewed) almost every year by the floods. Being newly deposited, it is light-coloured, sandy/loamy, and very fertile (renewed each year), making it ideal for intensive agriculture. (This contrasts with the 'Bhangar' — the older alluvium of the higher terraces, above the flood level, which is somewhat less fertile.) Understanding Khadar (the new, fertile, flood-renewed alluvium) is a prelims point. Khadar is the newer, very fertile alluvium of the Northern Plains, renewed by floods each year.

stem: The narrow belt of pebbles and gravels at the foot of the Shiwaliks, where the rivers descending from the mountains disappear underground, is called the:
solution: The Bhabar is the narrow belt (about 8–16 km wide) of coarse pebbles, gravels, and stones deposited at the foot of the Shiwaliks (where the Himalayan foothills meet the plains). Here, the streams and rivers descending from the mountains deposit their heavy load of coarse material, and — because the ground is so porous (pebbly) — the rivers disappear/sink underground (their flow goes below the surface). Below the Bhabar (to its south) lies the Terai belt, where these streams re-emerge. Understanding the Bhabar (pebbly belt where rivers go underground) is a prelims point. The Bhabar is the narrow pebbly belt at the foot of the Shiwaliks, where rivers disappear underground.

stem: The marshy, wet, forested belt lying south of the Bhabar, where the underground streams re-emerge, is called the:
solution: The Terai is the belt of marshy, wet, low-lying land lying just to the south of the Bhabar. Here, the streams and rivers that had disappeared underground in the porous Bhabar re-emerge at the surface, making the area wet, swampy, and (formerly) covered with thick forests and rich wildlife. Much of the Terai has since been cleared and drained for agriculture and settlement (it is now an important farming area). Understanding the Terai (the wet, marshy belt south of the Bhabar) is a prelims point. The Terai is the marshy, wet belt south of the Bhabar, where the underground streams re-emerge.

stem: The Peninsular Plateau of India is composed mainly of two broad divisions: the Central Highlands and the:
solution: The Peninsular Plateau of India is composed of two broad divisions: (1) the Central Highlands — the part lying to the north of the Narmada river, covering a large area of the Malwa plateau (bounded by the Aravallis on the north-west and the Vindhyas); and (2) the Deccan Plateau — the large triangular plateau lying to the south of the Narmada, covering most of the southern peninsula, bordered by the Western Ghats and the Eastern Ghats. Together these make up the ancient, stable Peninsular Plateau. Understanding the two divisions of the Peninsular Plateau (Central Highlands and Deccan Plateau) is a prelims point. The Peninsular Plateau consists of the Central Highlands (north of the Narmada) and the Deccan Plateau (south of it).

stem: The black soil (regur), ideal for growing cotton, found over a large part of the Deccan Plateau, was formed from:
solution: The black soil (called 'regur' or black cotton soil), found over a large part of the Deccan Plateau (especially Maharashtra, and parts of Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, and Karnataka), was formed from the weathering of the volcanic (basaltic) lava rocks known as the 'Deccan Traps'. Millions of years ago, huge outpourings of lava spread over this region, and the basalt rock, on weathering, gave rise to the fertile, moisture-retaining black soil — which is ideal for growing cotton (hence 'black cotton soil'). Understanding that the Deccan's black soil comes from volcanic (basaltic) lava is a prelims point. The black cotton soil (regur) of the Deccan formed from the weathering of volcanic basaltic lava (the Deccan Traps).

stem: The Peninsular Plateau is bordered on its western and eastern edges by two hill ranges called the:
solution: The Peninsular Plateau (specifically the Deccan Plateau) is bordered on its western edge by the Western Ghats and on its eastern edge by the Eastern Ghats — two hill ranges that run roughly parallel to the western and eastern coasts. The Western Ghats are higher, more continuous, and steeper; the Eastern Ghats are lower, more broken (dissected by rivers), and discontinuous. The two Ghats meet in the south (in the Nilgiri Hills). The plateau slopes generally from west to east (which is why most of its rivers flow eastward to the Bay of Bengal). Understanding the Western and Eastern Ghats (edges of the plateau) is a prelims point. The Peninsular Plateau is bordered by the Western Ghats (west) and the Eastern Ghats (east).

stem: Of the two, the __________ Ghats are higher, more continuous, and cannot be easily crossed except through passes.
solution: The Western Ghats are higher, more continuous (unbroken), and steeper than the Eastern Ghats, and they can only be crossed through certain passes (like the Thal Ghat, Bhor Ghat, and Pal Ghat). The Western Ghats run continuously along the western edge of the plateau (parallel to the west coast), rising to greater heights (their peaks generally 900–1600 m, higher in the south), and they cause heavy orographic rainfall on their windward (western) side by blocking the south-west monsoon. (The Eastern Ghats, by contrast, are lower, discontinuous, and much dissected by the rivers that cut through them.) Understanding that the Western Ghats are higher and more continuous than the Eastern Ghats is a prelims point. The Western Ghats are higher, more continuous, and crossed only through passes, unlike the lower, broken Eastern Ghats.

stem: The highest peak of the Western Ghats (and of Peninsular India) is:
solution: Anai Mudi (Anamudi), at about 2,695 m, is the highest peak of the Western Ghats and of the whole of Peninsular (southern) India. It is located in the Anaimalai Hills, in Kerala. (Other notable peaks: Dodabetta in the Nilgiri Hills; Guru Shikhar is the highest peak of the Aravalli range.) Understanding that Anai Mudi is the highest peak of the Western Ghats/Peninsular India is a prelims point. Anai Mudi (Anamudi) is the highest peak of the Western Ghats and of Peninsular India.

stem: The oldest fold mountain range in India (now much worn down/eroded), lying in the north-west of the Peninsular Plateau (mainly in Rajasthan), is the:
solution: The Aravalli Range is one of the oldest fold mountain ranges in India (and among the oldest in the world). It lies in the north-western part of the Peninsular Plateau, running mainly through Rajasthan (from Gujarat toward Delhi). Being extremely old, the Aravallis have been greatly worn down (eroded) over the ages, so they are now low, rounded, and broken hills (mere relics of once-lofty mountains). Their highest peak is Guru Shikhar (on Mount Abu). Understanding the Aravallis (India's oldest, much-eroded fold mountains) is a prelims point. The Aravalli Range, in the north-west of the Peninsula, is one of the oldest (and now much-worn-down) fold mountain ranges in India.

stem: The Peninsular Plateau generally slopes from west to east, which is why most of its large rivers (like the Godavari and Krishna) flow toward the:
solution: The Peninsular Plateau has a general slope from west to east (it is higher on the west, along the Western Ghats, and lower toward the east). Because of this eastward slope, most of the large peninsular rivers — such as the Godavari, the Krishna, the Kaveri, and the Mahanadi — flow from west to east, across the plateau, and drain into the Bay of Bengal (in the east). (Only a few peninsular rivers, notably the Narmada and the Tapi, flow westward into the Arabian Sea, along rift valleys.) Understanding that the plateau's eastward slope sends most rivers to the Bay of Bengal is a prelims point. The Peninsular Plateau slopes west to east, so most of its rivers flow eastward into the Bay of Bengal.

stem: The two major peninsular rivers that are exceptions, flowing WESTWARD into the Arabian Sea (through rift valleys), are the Narmada and the:
solution: The two major peninsular rivers that flow westward (as exceptions to the general eastward flow) into the Arabian Sea are the Narmada and the Tapi (Tapti). Both flow through rift valleys (long, narrow troughs formed by faulting/down-slipping of the land between roughly parallel faults) — the Narmada flowing between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges, and the Tapi to the south of it. Because they flow through these steep-sided rift valleys, they do not form deltas at their mouths (they form estuaries instead). Understanding that the Narmada and Tapi flow west (through rift valleys) is a prelims point. The Narmada and the Tapi are the peninsular rivers that flow westward into the Arabian Sea, through rift valleys.

stem: The Indian Desert (the Thar Desert) lies in which part of India?
solution: The Indian Desert (the Thar Desert, or the Great Indian Desert) lies in the north-western part of India, mainly in the state of Rajasthan (extending to the west of the Aravalli Hills), and into parts of Gujarat, Punjab, and Haryana (and across the border into Pakistan). It is a hot, dry, sandy region with very low and erratic rainfall (generally below 25 cm a year), sand dunes, and sparse, drought-resistant vegetation. The Luni is the only significant river of this region (an inland/ephemeral river). Understanding that the Thar Desert lies in the north-west (Rajasthan) is a prelims point. The Indian (Thar) Desert lies in the north-western part of India, mainly in Rajasthan.

stem: The Coastal Plains of India are divided into the Western Coastal Plains and the Eastern Coastal Plains. The Eastern Coastal Plains are __________ than the Western Coastal Plains.
solution: The Eastern Coastal Plains (along the Bay of Bengal) are wider (broader) than the Western Coastal Plains (along the Arabian Sea). The Eastern Coastal Plains are broad and level, and they include the large, fertile deltas built by the great east-flowing peninsular rivers (the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri) — so they are sometimes called the 'Northern Circars' (north) and the 'Coromandel Coast' (south). The Western Coastal Plains, by contrast, are narrow (squeezed between the Western Ghats and the sea). Understanding that the Eastern Coastal Plains are wider than the Western is a prelims point. The Eastern Coastal Plains are wider (broader) than the narrow Western Coastal Plains.

stem: The Western Coastal Plain is a narrow plain that lies between the __________ and the Arabian Sea.
solution: The Western Coastal Plain is a narrow strip of plain that lies between the Western Ghats (on the east) and the Arabian Sea (on the west). Because it is squeezed between the steep Western Ghats and the sea, it is narrow. It is divided into sections with different names — from north to south: the Konkan coast (Maharashtra/Goa), the Kannad/Karnataka coast, and the Malabar coast (Kerala). The rivers here are short and swift and do not form deltas (they form estuaries), and the Malabar coast has distinctive lagoons/backwaters (like the Kerala backwaters). Understanding that the Western Coastal Plain lies between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea is a prelims point. The Western Coastal Plain is the narrow plain between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea.

stem: Assertion (A): The Himalayas are prone to earthquakes. Reason (R): The Himalayas are young fold mountains formed by the ongoing collision of the Indian and Asian plates, so the region is tectonically active. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the Himalayas (and the surrounding regions) are prone to earthquakes. And the reason is (R) that the Himalayas are young fold mountains, formed by the collision of the northward-moving Indian plate with the Asian plate — a collision that is still ongoing (the Indian plate continues to push into Asia). This continuing tectonic activity (the plates grinding and building up stress) makes the region tectonically active and therefore earthquake-prone. So R correctly explains A. Understanding this link (young, still-colliding fold mountains → earthquakes) is a prelims point. The Himalayas are earthquake-prone because they are young fold mountains formed by the ongoing collision of the Indian and Asian plates.

stem: The mountain range to the north of the Himalayas, containing K2 (Godwin Austen) — the highest peak in India's claimed territory and the second highest in the world — is the:
solution: The Karakoram Range lies to the north of the main Himalayas (in the trans-Himalayan region, in the northernmost part of India's territory — the Kashmir/Ladakh region). It contains K2 (also called Godwin Austen), which at about 8,611 m is the second highest peak in the world and the highest peak in India's claimed territory (though it lies in the Pakistan-administered part of Kashmir). The Karakoram also has some of the world's largest glaciers outside the polar regions (like the Siachen and Baltoro glaciers). Understanding the Karakoram (northern range with K2) is a prelims point. The Karakoram Range, north of the Himalayas, contains K2 — the second highest peak in the world.

stem: The high, cold, dry plateau region in the northernmost part of India (a 'cold desert' between the Karakoram and the Himalayas) is the __________ region.
solution: The Ladakh region is a high, cold, dry plateau in the northernmost part of India, lying between the Karakoram Range and the Great Himalayas (in the trans-Himalayan zone). Because it lies in the rain shadow of the Himalayas (which block the monsoon), it is extremely dry — a 'cold desert' — with very little rainfall, freezing temperatures, and a bare, rugged, high-altitude landscape (the Indus river flows through it). Leh is its main town. Understanding Ladakh (India's high cold desert) is a prelims point. Ladakh is the high, cold, dry plateau ('cold desert') in the northernmost part of India, between the Karakoram and the Himalayas.

stem: The Himalayan rivers (like the Indus, Sutlej, and Brahmaputra) that are older than the Himalayas themselves — having cut deep gorges as the mountains rose around them — are described as __________ rivers.
solution: The major Himalayan rivers (such as the Indus, the Sutlej, and the Brahmaputra) are described as antecedent rivers — meaning they are older than (they existed before) the mountains they now cut through. As the Himalayas were slowly uplifted, these pre-existing rivers were able to keep cutting down (eroding) at about the same rate as the land rose, so they maintained their courses right across the rising mountains, carving deep gorges through them. This is evidence that these rivers pre-date (are 'antecedent' to) the present Himalayan ranges. Understanding antecedent rivers (older than the mountains, cutting gorges) is a prelims point. Antecedent rivers (like the Indus and Brahmaputra) are older than the Himalayas and cut deep gorges as the mountains rose.

stem: The mineral-rich plateau in the eastern part of the Peninsular Plateau (in the Jharkhand region), famous as the 'storehouse of minerals' of India, is the __________ Plateau.
solution: The Chotanagpur Plateau, located in the eastern part of the Peninsular Plateau (mainly in Jharkhand, and parts of Odisha, West Bengal, and Chhattisgarh), is famous as the 'storehouse of minerals' (the mineral heartland) of India. It is very rich in minerals — coal, iron ore, mica, bauxite, copper, and many others — which have made it a major centre of mining and heavy industry in India. Understanding the Chotanagpur Plateau (India's mineral storehouse) is a prelims point. The Chotanagpur Plateau (in Jharkhand) is the mineral-rich 'storehouse of minerals' of India.

stem: The two roughly east-west ranges that border the Narmada rift valley — the Vindhya Range (to the north) and the __________ Range (to the south) — separate northern India from the Deccan.
solution: The Narmada river flows westward through a rift valley bordered by two roughly east-west ranges: the Vindhya Range to its north and the Satpura Range to its south. These ranges (the Vindhyas and the Satpuras), running east-west across central India, act as a barrier/divide separating the northern plains and Central Highlands from the Deccan Plateau to the south (they are traditionally regarded as the divide between North and South India). Understanding the Vindhya and Satpura ranges (bordering the Narmada) is a prelims point. The Satpura Range (with the Vindhya Range) borders the Narmada valley and helps separate northern India from the Deccan.

stem: The Meghalaya Plateau (in the north-east) is made up of three hill groups: the Garo, the Khasi, and the __________ Hills.
solution: The Meghalaya Plateau (also called the Shillong Plateau) in north-eastern India is made up of three hill groups, from west to east: the Garo Hills, the Khasi Hills, and the Jaintia Hills. (These are named after the tribal groups living there.) This plateau — actually an eastward extension of the Peninsular Plateau, separated from it by a gap — receives extremely heavy rainfall (Mawsynram and Cherrapunji, among the wettest places on Earth, are on the Khasi Hills). Understanding the three hill groups of the Meghalaya Plateau (Garo, Khasi, Jaintia) is a prelims point. The Meghalaya Plateau consists of the Garo, Khasi, and Jaintia Hills.

stem: The Nilgiri Hills, where the Western Ghats and the Eastern Ghats meet, contain the hill station of:
solution: The Nilgiri Hills (meaning 'Blue Mountains'), located where the Western Ghats and the Eastern Ghats meet (in the south, at the junction of Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Karnataka), contain the famous hill station of Ooty (Udhagamandalam or Ootacamund). Dodabetta, the highest peak of the Nilgiris, is also here. (Shimla, Nainital, and Darjeeling are hill stations of the Himalayas.) Understanding that the Nilgiris (junction of the two Ghats) contain Ooty is a prelims point. The Nilgiri Hills, where the Western and Eastern Ghats meet, contain the hill station of Ooty.

stem: The gap/pass in the Western Ghats (in the south) that provides an important route between the west coast (Kerala) and the interior (Tamil Nadu) is the:
solution: The Palghat Gap (Palakkad Gap) is a low gap/pass in the Western Ghats in the south (between the Nilgiri Hills to the north and the Anaimalai Hills to the south). It provides an important natural route (for roads and railways) between the west coast (Kerala) and the interior/east (Tamil Nadu and the rest of the peninsula), through the otherwise continuous barrier of the Western Ghats. Understanding the Palghat Gap (key pass in the southern Western Ghats) is a prelims point. The Palghat (Palakkad) Gap is the important pass in the Western Ghats linking Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

stem: The largest river of the Peninsular Plateau, sometimes called the 'Dakshin Ganga' (Ganga of the South), is the:
solution: The Godavari is the largest river of the Peninsular Plateau (and the second longest river in India after the Ganga). Because of its length and importance, it is often called the 'Dakshin Ganga' (the Ganga of the South). It rises in the Western Ghats (in Maharashtra) and flows south-east across the Deccan to drain into the Bay of Bengal, forming a large delta. Understanding that the Godavari is the largest peninsular river ('Dakshin Ganga') is a prelims point. The Godavari is the largest river of the Peninsula, called the 'Dakshin Ganga'.

stem: The area of land lying between two rivers (like the fertile land between the Ganga and the Yamuna) is called a:
solution: A doab is the area/tract of land lying between two rivers (the word 'doab' means 'two waters'). The most famous example is the Ganga-Yamuna Doab — the fertile plain lying between the Ganga and the Yamuna rivers in the Northern Plains. Doabs are typically very fertile and well-watered (lying between two rivers), and hence important agricultural areas. Understanding the doab (land between two rivers) is a prelims point. A doab is the land lying between two rivers (like the Ganga-Yamuna Doab).

stem: The largest brackish-water coastal lagoon in India, located on the eastern coast in Odisha, is:
solution: Chilika Lake, located on the eastern (Bay of Bengal) coast in Odisha, is the largest brackish-water (salt-water) coastal lagoon in India (and one of the largest in the world). It is a shallow lagoon separated from the sea by a sandbar/spit, and it is an important habitat for migratory birds and other wildlife (a Ramsar wetland site). It is a depositional coastal feature. Understanding that Chilika (Odisha) is India's largest coastal lagoon is a prelims point. Chilika Lake, in Odisha, is the largest brackish-water coastal lagoon in India.

stem: The famous 'backwaters' (network of lagoons and lakes, locally called 'kayals') are a feature of the __________ coast.
solution: The famous backwaters — a network of interconnected lagoons, lakes, and channels running parallel to the coast (locally called 'kayals') — are a distinctive feature of the Malabar Coast (the southern part of the Western Coastal Plain, in Kerala). These backwaters (like the Vembanad Lake) are used for fishing, inland navigation, and tourism (the Kerala backwaters are a major tourist attraction). Understanding that the backwaters (kayals) are a feature of the Malabar/Kerala coast is a prelims point. The backwaters (kayals) are a feature of the Malabar (Kerala) coast.

stem: The northern part of the Western Coastal Plain (in Maharashtra and Goa) is called the __________ coast.
solution: The Konkan Coast is the northern part of the Western Coastal Plain, running along Maharashtra and Goa. (The Western Coastal Plain, from north to south, is divided into: the Konkan Coast — Maharashtra/Goa; the Kannad/Karnataka Coast — Karnataka; and the Malabar Coast — Kerala.) The Konkan coast is a narrow, indented plain along the Arabian Sea. Understanding the Konkan coast (northern Western Coastal Plain) is a prelims point. The Konkan Coast is the northern part of the Western Coastal Plain (Maharashtra and Goa).

stem: The southern part of the Eastern Coastal Plain (in Tamil Nadu) is known as the __________ coast.
solution: The Coromandel Coast is the southern part of the Eastern Coastal Plain, running along Tamil Nadu (and southern Andhra Pradesh), along the Bay of Bengal. (The northern part of the Eastern Coastal Plain, in Andhra Pradesh/Odisha, is called the 'Northern Circars'.) The Coromandel coast receives much of its rain from the retreating (north-east) monsoon in winter. Understanding the Coromandel coast (southern Eastern Coastal Plain, Tamil Nadu) is a prelims point. The Coromandel Coast is the southern part of the Eastern Coastal Plain (Tamil Nadu).

stem: The large area of salt marshes and mudflats in the north-west (Gujarat), which is flooded in the wet season and becomes a salt-crusted flat in the dry season, is the:
solution: The Rann of Kutch is a large area of salt marshes, mudflats, and salt flats in the north-western part of India, in Gujarat (near the border with Pakistan). It is a low, flat area that gets flooded/marshy with sea water and rainwater during the wet (monsoon) season, and then dries out into a vast, glistening salt-encrusted flat (a salt desert) during the dry season. It is divided into the Great Rann and the Little Rann. (The Little Rann is a habitat of the wild ass.) Understanding the Rann of Kutch (the seasonal salt marsh/flat of Gujarat) is a prelims point. The Rann of Kutch, in Gujarat, is a salt marsh that floods in the wet season and dries into a salt flat in the dry season.

stem: The peninsular rivers that flow westward through rift valleys (like the Narmada and Tapi) form __________ at their mouths, rather than deltas.
solution: The peninsular rivers that flow westward through rift valleys — the Narmada and the Tapi — form estuaries at their mouths (where they meet the Arabian Sea), rather than deltas. This is because they flow through steep-sided, narrow rift valleys with a swift flow and hard rock, so they do not carry and deposit the large amount of loose sediment needed to build a delta; instead, their mouths remain as funnel-shaped estuaries (where the river widens into the sea). (In contrast, the east-flowing peninsular rivers, like the Godavari and Krishna, do form large deltas on the eastern coast.) Understanding that the Narmada and Tapi form estuaries (not deltas) is a prelims point. The west-flowing rift-valley rivers (Narmada, Tapi) form estuaries, not deltas, at their mouths.

stem: The Deccan Traps (the extensive volcanic basalt rocks of the Deccan) were formed by:
options: Massive outpourings/eruptions of lava in the geological past
solution: The Deccan Traps are the extensive area of volcanic basalt rocks that cover a large part of the Deccan Plateau (much of Maharashtra and adjoining areas). They were formed by massive outpourings/eruptions of lava (fluid basaltic lava) in the geological past (around the end of the Cretaceous period, about 65 million years ago): the lava flowed out from cracks/fissures and spread over vast areas, cooling and solidifying in layers (the step-like 'trap' structure), building up thick sheets of basalt. On weathering, these basalt rocks give the fertile black soil. Understanding that the Deccan Traps formed from lava eruptions is a prelims point. The Deccan Traps are volcanic basalt rocks formed by massive outpourings of lava in the geological past.

stem: The Northern Plains are sometimes divided (from west to east) into the Punjab Plains, the Ganga Plains, and the __________ Plains (in Assam).
solution: The Northern Plains are sometimes divided, from west to east, into three sections: the Punjab Plains (in the west, formed by the Indus and its tributaries), the Ganga Plains (in the centre, formed by the Ganga and its tributaries — the largest section, spread across many states), and the Brahmaputra Plains (in the east, in Assam, formed by the Brahmaputra river). Each is built by the alluvium of its respective river system. Understanding the three sections of the Northern Plains (Punjab, Ganga, Brahmaputra) is a prelims point. The Northern Plains are divided into the Punjab Plains, the Ganga Plains, and the Brahmaputra Plains (in Assam).

stem: The Andaman & Nicobar Islands and the Lakshadweep differ in origin: the Lakshadweep are __________ islands.
solution: The Lakshadweep Islands (in the Arabian Sea) are coral islands — they are built up by corals (tiny marine organisms whose limestone skeletons form reefs and atolls). This is in contrast to the Andaman & Nicobar Islands (in the Bay of Bengal), which are of tectonic and volcanic origin (elevations of submerged mountain ranges, in a tectonically active zone). So the two island groups have different origins: the Lakshadweep are coral, while the Andaman & Nicobar are tectonic/volcanic. Understanding that the Lakshadweep are coral islands is a prelims point. The Lakshadweep are coral islands (unlike the tectonic/volcanic Andaman & Nicobar Islands).

stem: Which physiographic division of India is the youngest, and geologically the most unstable/active (prone to earthquakes)?
solution: The Himalayan (Northern) Mountains are the youngest physiographic division of India and geologically the most unstable/active (prone to earthquakes). They are young fold mountains, still being uplifted by the ongoing collision of the Indian and Asian plates, which keeps the region tectonically active and earthquake-prone. (In sharp contrast, the Peninsular Plateau is the oldest and most stable division — a rigid ancient shield.) Understanding that the Himalayas are the youngest and most tectonically active division is a prelims point. The Himalayan Mountains are the youngest and most geologically active (earthquake-prone) physiographic division of India.

stem: The variety of India's physiographic divisions is valuable because each provides different resources — the mountains give __________, the plains give fertile farmland, and the plateaus give minerals.
options: rivers, forests, and tourism (and act as a climatic barrier)
solution: India's varied physiographic divisions are valuable because each provides different resources and benefits: the mountains (Himalayas) give perennial rivers (fed by snow and glaciers), forests and timber, medicinal plants, hydroelectric potential, tourism (hill stations, pilgrimage), and act as a climatic barrier (blocking cold winds and the monsoon) and a defence barrier; the Northern Plains give deep, fertile alluvial soil and abundant water — the farmland that feeds the nation; and the Peninsular Plateau gives minerals (coal, iron ore, etc.), building stone, and (in places) fertile black soil. The coasts give ports, fisheries, and salt, and the islands and deserts have their own resources too. This diversity of resources, arising from the varied physiography, is a great asset for India. Understanding the resource value of the different physiographic divisions is a prelims-relevant point. India's varied physiography is valuable because the mountains give rivers/forests/tourism, the plains give farmland, and the plateaus give minerals.

stem: The highest peak in India (and the third highest in the world), located in Sikkim, is:
solution: Kanchenjunga, in Sikkim, is the highest peak located within India, and the third highest mountain in the world (Mount Everest and K2 lie outside India's present territory).

stem: The northernmost, highest range of the Himalayas, containing the loftiest peaks, is the:
solution: The Himadri or Greater Himalayas is the northernmost and highest range of the Himalayas, containing the loftiest peaks with perennial snow.

stem: The southernmost, lowest range of the Himalayas, made of unconsolidated sediments, is the:
solution: The Shiwaliks form the southernmost and lowest range of the Himalayas, composed of unconsolidated sediments brought down by rivers from the higher ranges.

stem: The middle range of the Himalayas, lying between the Himadri and the Shiwaliks, is the:
solution: The Himachal or Lesser Himalayas lies between the Greater Himalayas (Himadri) and the Shiwaliks, and includes famous ranges like the Pir Panjal and hill stations like Shimla and Mussoorie.

stem: The flat-floored structural valleys lying between the Lesser Himalayas and the Shiwaliks are called:
solution: Duns are the longitudinal, flat-floored structural valleys formed between the Lesser Himalayas and the Shiwaliks; examples include Dehra Dun and the Kotli Dun.

stem: The narrow belt of pebbles and gravels at the foot of the Shiwaliks, where rivers disappear underground, is called the:
solution: The Bhabar is a narrow belt of pebbles and gravels deposited at the foot of the Shiwaliks; here the streams disappear and flow underground before re-emerging in the Terai belt to the south.

stem: The marshy, wet, forested belt lying south of the Bhabar, where the streams re-emerge, is the:
solution: The Terai is the marshy, wet and thickly forested belt lying south of the Bhabar, where the underground streams re-emerge at the surface.

stem: In the Northern Plains, the older alluvium, which forms terraces above the flood plains, is called:
solution: Bhangar is the older alluvium in the Northern Plains, forming terraces above the level of the flood plains; it often contains kankar (lime nodules).

stem: In the Northern Plains, the newer, younger alluvium deposited by floods each year is called:
solution: Khadar is the newer, younger alluvium of the flood plains, deposited by rivers during floods; it is renewed almost every year and is very fertile.

stem: The Northern Plains of India are formed by the alluvial deposits of the Indus, the Ganga and the:
solution: The Northern Plains are formed by the alluvium brought down and deposited by the three great river systems — the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra — and their tributaries.

stem: The Peninsular Plateau of India is composed mainly of:
options: Old, hard igneous and metamorphic rocks
solution: The Peninsular Plateau is composed mainly of old, hard igneous and metamorphic rocks; it is one of the oldest and most stable landmasses, formed from a part of the ancient Gondwana land.

stem: The Deccan Traps, the extensive basalt rocks of the peninsula, were formed by:
solution: The Deccan Traps are extensive plateaus of basaltic rock formed by huge volcanic (lava) eruptions long ago; the weathering of this basalt gives rise to the black cotton (regur) soil.

stem: The Peninsular Plateau is bordered on its western and eastern sides by the:
solution: The Peninsular Plateau is bordered on the west by the Western Ghats and on the east by the Eastern Ghats, which rise along its margins.

stem: Of the two, the __________ Ghats are higher, more continuous and receive more rainfall.
solution: The Western Ghats are higher, more continuous, and receive more rainfall than the Eastern Ghats, which are lower and broken up by the rivers that flow to the Bay of Bengal.

stem: Assertion (A): The Himalayas are prone to earthquakes. Reason (R): They are young fold mountains, still rising, located along the boundary of moving tectonic plates.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: The Himalayas are prone to earthquakes because they are young, still-rising fold mountains formed at the collision boundary of the Indian and Eurasian plates, where the crust is unstable — R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): The Northern Plains are among the most densely populated regions of India. Reason (R): Their fertile alluvial soil, level land and abundant water make them ideal for agriculture and settlement.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: The Northern Plains are densely populated because their fertile alluvial soil, flat land and abundant water support intensive agriculture and dense settlement — R explains A.

stem: The oldest fold mountain range in India, now much worn down, running through Rajasthan, is the:
solution: The Aravalli Range is one of the oldest fold mountain ranges in the world, now greatly worn down by erosion; it runs through Rajasthan and Gujarat.

stem: The two roughly east-west ranges that border the Narmada valley are the Vindhyas (to the north) and the:
solution: The Narmada river flows westward through a rift valley bordered by the Vindhya Range to the north and the Satpura Range to the south.

stem: The peninsular rivers that flow westward through rift valleys to the Arabian Sea are the Narmada and the:
solution: The Narmada and the Tapi (Tapti) are the two major peninsular rivers that flow westward through rift valleys into the Arabian Sea, unlike most peninsular rivers which flow east to the Bay of Bengal.

stem: The Peninsular Plateau generally slopes from west to east, which is why most of its major rivers flow:
options: Eastward into the Bay of Bengal
solution: The Peninsular Plateau generally slopes from west to east, which is why most of its major rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Mahanadi) flow eastward into the Bay of Bengal.

stem: The largest river of the Peninsular Plateau, sometimes called the 'Dakshin Ganga', is the:
solution: The Godavari is the largest river of the Peninsular Plateau; because of its length and size, it is sometimes called the 'Dakshin Ganga' (the Ganga of the South).

stem: The mineral-rich plateau in the eastern part of the Peninsula, covering Jharkhand and nearby areas, is the:
solution: The Chota Nagpur Plateau, in the eastern part of the Peninsula (Jharkhand and adjoining areas), is very rich in minerals like coal and iron ore, making it India's mineral heartland.

stem: The Nilgiri Hills, where the Western Ghats and the Eastern Ghats meet, are located in the:
solution: The Nilgiri Hills, where the Western and Eastern Ghats join, are located in the southern part of the Peninsula; Ooty (Udhagamandalam) is a famous hill station there.

stem: Match the range with its region: (i) Aravalli (ii) Satpura (iii) Western Ghats — (a) west coast border (b) Rajasthan (c) south of Narmada:
solution: The Aravalli range runs through Rajasthan, the Satpura range lies south of the Narmada, and the Western Ghats border the west coast.

stem: The Coastal Plains of India are divided into the Western Coastal Plain and the:
solution: The Coastal Plains of India are divided into the narrow Western Coastal Plain (along the Arabian Sea) and the broader Eastern Coastal Plain (along the Bay of Bengal).

stem: The Western Coastal Plain is a narrow plain lying between the Western Ghats and the:
solution: The Western Coastal Plain is a narrow strip of land lying between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea, running along the western coast of India.

stem: The famous 'backwaters' (a network of lagoons and lakes) are found along the coast of:
solution: The famous backwaters — a network of interconnected lagoons, lakes and canals — are found along the Malabar coast of Kerala on the Western Coastal Plain.

stem: The largest brackish-water coastal lagoon in India, located in Odisha, is:
solution: Chilika Lake, in Odisha on the eastern coast, is the largest brackish-water coastal lagoon in India, an important habitat for birds and other wildlife.

stem: The high, cold, dry plateau region in the northernmost part of India, beyond the Great Himalayas, is:
solution: Ladakh, a high, cold desert lying in the Trans-Himalayan (Tibetan plateau) region beyond the Great Himalayas, is the northernmost cold, dry plateau region of India.

stem: The mountain range to the north of the Great Himalayas, containing the peak K2, is the:
solution: The Karakoram Range lies to the north of the Great Himalayas and contains K2 (Godwin Austen), the highest peak in the Indian subcontinent (though outside India's current control) and the second highest in the world.

stem: The Himalayan rivers (like the Indus, Sutlej and Brahmaputra) are older than the Himalayas, cutting deep gorges, which shows they are:
solution: Some Himalayan rivers, like the Indus, Sutlej and Brahmaputra, are 'antecedent' rivers — older than the Himalayas — which continued to cut down as the mountains rose, forming deep gorges.

stem: The Meghalaya Plateau (in the north-east) contains the wettest places on Earth, namely:
solution: The Meghalaya Plateau in the north-east contains Cherrapunji and Mawsynram, among the wettest places on Earth, receiving extremely heavy monsoon rainfall.

stem: The area of land lying between two rivers, such as the fertile land between the Ganga and the Yamuna, is called a:
solution: A doab is the area of land lying between two rivers; the fertile land between the Ganga and the Yamuna is the well-known Ganga-Yamuna doab.

stem: The large area of salt marshes and mudflats in the north-western part of Gujarat is the:
solution: The Rann of Kutch is a large area of salt marshes and mudflats in the north-western part of Gujarat, flooded in the monsoon and turning into a salt desert in the dry season.

stem: The Andaman & Nicobar Islands and the Lakshadweep differ in origin: the Lakshadweep islands are __________ islands.
solution: The Lakshadweep Islands in the Arabian Sea are coral islands (built by coral polyps), whereas the Andaman & Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal are largely of volcanic and tectonic origin.

stem: Which physiographic division of India is the youngest, geologically?
options: The Northern Plains and the Himalayas
solution: The Himalayas and the Northern Plains are the youngest physiographic divisions of India geologically; the Himalayas formed in the recent geological past, and the plains were built up even more recently by river deposition.

stem: The Himalayas are young fold mountains formed by the:
options: Collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates
solution: The Himalayas are young fold mountains formed by the collision of the northward-moving Indian plate with the Eurasian plate, which folded the sediments of the ancient Tethys sea into mountains.

stem: The ancient sea, in whose sediments the Himalayas were folded, was called the:
solution: The Himalayas were formed by the folding of the sediments deposited in the ancient Tethys Sea, which lay between the Indian plate and the Eurasian plate before their collision.

stem: The Indian landmass is broadly divided into the Himalayan mountains, the Northern Plains, the Peninsular Plateau, the Indian Desert, the coastal plains and the:
solution: India's physiography is broadly divided into six major divisions: the Himalayan Mountains, the Northern Plains, the Peninsular Plateau, the Indian Desert, the Coastal Plains, and the Islands.

stem: The oldest and most stable landmass of India, part of the ancient Gondwana land, is the:
solution: The Peninsular Plateau is the oldest and most stable landmass of India, being a part of the ancient Gondwana land, composed of old crystalline igneous and metamorphic rocks.

stem: The Northern Plains are famous for being extremely __________, supporting intensive agriculture.
solution: The Northern Plains are famous for being extremely fertile, being made up of rich alluvial soil deposited by rivers, which supports intensive agriculture and dense population.

stem: The northern part of the Western Coastal Plain (in Maharashtra and Goa) is known as the:
solution: The Western Coastal Plain is divided into the Konkan coast (north, in Maharashtra and Goa), the Kanara coast (Karnataka), and the Malabar coast (south, in Kerala).

stem: The southern part of the Eastern Coastal Plain (in Tamil Nadu) is known as the:
solution: The Eastern Coastal Plain is divided into the Northern Circars (north) and the Coromandel coast (south, in Tamil Nadu), along the Bay of Bengal.

stem: The hilly ranges of the north-eastern Himalayas (in Arunachal Pradesh and beyond) are collectively called the:
solution: The Purvanchal (Eastern Hills), including the Patkai, Naga, Manipur and Mizo hills, are the hilly ranges of the north-eastern Himalayas where the range bends sharply southward.

stem: The black soil (regur), ideal for growing cotton, found on the Peninsular Plateau is formed by the weathering of:
solution: The black cotton soil (regur) of the Peninsular Plateau, ideal for growing cotton, is formed by the weathering of the basaltic lava rocks of the Deccan Traps.

stem: The variety of India's physiographic divisions is valuable because it:
options: Gives India a rich diversity of relief, soils, climate, resources and agriculture
solution: The variety of India's physiographic divisions — mountains, plains, plateaus, deserts, coasts and islands — gives the country a rich diversity of relief, soils, climate, natural vegetation, minerals and agricultural possibilities.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Structure and Physiography' is that:
options: India has a diverse physiography of mountains, plains, plateaus, deserts, coasts and islands shaped by its geological history
solution: The chapter concludes that India has a diverse physiography — the Himalayas, the Northern Plains, the Peninsular Plateau, the Indian Desert, the coastal plains and the islands — shaped by its long geological history, each division having distinct features and significance.
